artifacts.description: Build a theory of how applying a day-of-year-windowed weighted local linear regression with WIDE smoothing windows (half-window h = 45 days, i.e. +/- 45 days of pooling) to reconstruct daily dew-point temperature from daily minimum temperature produces extreme over-prediction errors (dew points above 35 C) that are confined almost entirely to a SINGLE calendar month (November), with essentially zero errors in adjacent months (October 0.027%, November 1.556%, December 0.018%, and only 50 exceedances in total across January to July), in the north-eastern Amazon lowlands of Peru. The puzzle is the sharpness: a smoothing window spanning +/- 45 days should smear any smoothly varying seasonal effect across October to December, so how can the failure be confined to one month? Consider in particular whether an ABRUPT physical transition - the onset of the Amazonian wet season, which occurs around October-November - can produce a sharp single-month failure in a model whose smoothing window is deliberately broad, because the underlying transition is discontinuous while the fitted model is smooth. Also consider alternative mechanisms that could concentrate error into one month: regime switching or bimodal humidity distributions at onset, discontinuous land-atmosphere coupling and evapotranspiration recycling at wet-season onset, rapid changes in cloud cover and nocturnal cooling that decouple minimum temperature from moisture, and statistical artefacts such as day-of-year boundary effects, leverage of extreme training anomalies, or heteroscedastic residuals concentrated at the transition.

s2_metadata.abstract: Stochastic weather generators are probabilistic tools used to simulate synthetic weather data whose statistics resemble those observed. These tools face difficulties when it comes to accurately simulating multiple meteorological variables in space and time, because they necessitate models that can capture the complex inter-variable and space-time dependencies. We propose a new multivariate space-time weather generator designed for regional-scale applications at a daily resolution, called MSTWeatherGen. This stochastic weather generator takes advantage of the recent development of multivariate space-time covariance functions to model and simulate different weather variables, including temperature, precipitation, wind speed, humidity, and solar radiation, across space and time. Specifically, we employ an approach that involves a non-linear and non-stationary marginal transformation of a multivariate Gaussian random field, characterized by a stationary and non-separable spatio-temporal multivariate cross-covariance function. To further address the time-varying nature of the weather variables, we split the time domain into states called weather types. The method is assessed on the Provence-Alpes-Côte-d’Azur region in France, which is characterized by heterogeneous topography and meteorological conditions. Evaluation results demonstrate the effectiveness of this new stochastic weather generator in reproducing a wide range of weather statistics, including highly non-linear indicators such as heat wave or fire weather index.
